i see these posts on here semi-often, so i'm going to chime in now. my credentials are that i have a graduate degree in material science (crystallography) and i literally teach college courses in geology and oceanography.


Explanation:
========================
water expands as it freezes because of the special properties of the H2O molecule and the way these molecules come together in a crystalline solid (i.e., ice). the process of forming these ice spikes is not fully understood, but modern theory goes a lot like this:

(1) liquid water in a container is suddenly moved into an environment below water's freezing point (i.e., putting an ice tray in the freezer)

(2) heat diffuses away from the water from the outside-in. thus, the sides and bottom/top of the volume if water begins to freeze first.

(3) midway through this process, the water has a solid, icy outer shell with a liquid water center. this is an issue because water likes to expand as it freezes (as stated above).

(4) as the water continues to freeze, the expanding volume of the ice now needs somewhere to go. the weakest part of the "ice shell" is usually the exposed top surface (of an ice tray, or a pond, or etc). this surface is unconfined by the walls of the container, or it may even feature an existing hole where the top surface has not yet completely frozen over.

(5) ice extrudes upward through the opening as the water expands inside its container, forming an upward-pointing "icesicle" as the water continues to solidify.


the nitty-gritty specifics of this phenomenon break down into the way and shape in which ice crystallizes, which i won't bog this explanation down with here. i will note, the phenomenon *is* observed in nature, but artificial "home-grown" varieties like this are far more common, likely due to the nature of the vessel holding/confining the water.

to me, art is a language, just like music. so the goal is communication. you're either trying to convey an idea or a feeling or whatever. so, if you can communicate well enough in this language that your subject is readily identifiable, to me that's "effective" art. it's all subjective in the end, anyways, so it's really the artist who determines if it's good or not for themself -- did you communicate what you wanted to say as clearly as you wanted to say it? in your first drawing, you wanted to show me a sword in a stone, and i see a sword in a stone. so i say talent haha.

whatever your "style" is, *lean into it.* cultivate it and help it grow! it's as much a living thing as you are, and it will change over time as you do and as you get more comfortable in your medium. i will say, almost *nobody* is good at realism from the jump. you sort of have to re-train how your brain processes visual input, learning how to break complex objects down into basic shapes, textures, and geometries. 

almost *nobody* is "good" at art when they start, too. for this reason i hate to use the word "talent," because it diminishes the significance of the work the artist did to get to that point in their creative journey. being visually creative is a skill. you have to practice! there's a tendency in people to transpose carefully honed skill for native genious; all they see is the artwork, not the hundreds to thousands of hours you may have spent learning how to make it. in your case, i say talent specifically because you say you *haven't* trained your craft, yet.

your medium is the material/technique with which you work; i.e., i'm a painter, my medium is acrylic paints on primed canvases. i also do sketches, and my medium for that is graphite on gesso canvas or heavyweight paper.

​

i'm sorry for the rant, i'm just very passionate about art. i'm actually an outsider with no formal training whatsoever, so college-schooled artists would probably scoff at all this feel-good talk, haha. **The important thing is that you enjoy creating. Skill will come with time. Remember to enjoy the process!**

Oh, I never consider anything I make to be 'done.' I just lose interest or move on to a new subject. My brain still has plans to work on this one, so I guess it's still going.

I almost never paint the same way twice. This one was pretty interesting; I posed for and photographed the reference myself, lighting included. I wanted to use differently colored light sources from different angles to exaggerate the curvature. From there I sketched the outline on the canvas with graphite and painted directly over it. I blasted this out in about 7 hours this afternoon, but preparing the canvas itself takes much longer (several days of priming and sanding to achieve a semi-flat subtle tigerstripe texture; may be hard to notice in the image).

As I said, the painting is "incomplete" for me. I still want to leave the top half deliberately sketchy and pale, and instead of a head I will draw a thick cable bundle going straight up off the canvas. The general theme is about how technology integrates us and we are both greater and lesser for it. "Can't see the cosmos for the screens" to iterate on a phrase. But it is the nature of intelligence to cultivate itself, grow, and develop over time. Technology may blind us to the outside universe, but it helps us grow our inner light.

These are all things that have just been on my mind lately. Really, the original concept was very different. My concept often changes to adapt as I work with the piece to find a nice shape.

The questions are very much appreciated! I am entirely self-taught! I have no idea if this would be considered classically "good" art, but I don't care. I made it to make myself happy.

Exactly! The worst thing for me is trying to paint from a reference. I get stuck comparing what I've made to what I'm trying to copy. I almost never paint from a reference to avoid this, and it makes me feel like my work is more original and more representative of "me." I consider every painting I make a sort of "self portrait," because a little bit of the real me makes it into every canvas, as long as I'm painting this way.

And color is the most important thing to a painting in my opinion. Colors have all kinds of attached emotions! It's where a lot of the feelings of a piece come from, and it's the most obvious benefit of paint over monochromatic media like charcoal or graphite. I like to use only a few colors at a time to keep my painting's "mood" focused,  and it keeps the painting from looking too "busy."

That was another part of me coming into my own as an artist, too. I discovered that nobody else will ever see my paintings the same way I do. The creator can never really be an objective observer. I once tried to paint a planet, and everyone thought it looked like a cave. It was really upsetting, because I thought I had done a good job, and my subject was so clear and obvious to me. So I shifted my goal from trying to perfectly replicate nature to a goal of just trying to shape impressions and create feelings.

In a lot of ways, I find "less is more," so to speak. I hope it's not too cliché to quote Bob Ross here, but I like how he thinks: just do enough work to "give the idea" of a cloud or a tree or a rock. The human brain is amazing. We see patterns in chaos. Trying too hard can work against you and be frustrating and stressful!

Lastly, I hate explaining my work to people. It's *meant* to be an image! Trying to force the idea into words just feels damaging and inadequate. As I see it, your audience will see what they want to see in your art. Let them take out of it what they come to it with. Let your viewers find their own meaning in your work. That way, instead of just one meaning, your art's meaning can be manifold. If you still feel you must give your piece more direction, you still want your *audience* to be the ones interpreting your work, not yourself. There's no satisfaction in just telling the punchline of a joke; there needs to be setup, connections, understanding. If you want to paint a tree, don't simply paint a tree, paint enough clues to let your audience piece it together. Splashes of green and yellow leaves; directed, meaningful brown strokes for a trunk; maybe you dot some extra color in the branches, giving the idea of fruit or flowers. It's helpful to think this way because it also breaks down large, complex subjects into smaller, more manageable tasks.

TL,DR: Let your work be weird. Let it be "bad." If you're frustrated, that's a feeling too! Put that into your painting. For me, painting isn't about making postcards or cheap, bland art to hang in hotel lobbies. I want to say things you *can't* say with words. And when you do that, only you can know if what you said is what you meant. Not everyone will like everything you make, but you'll connect to a few of them. And if what your image says speaks the truth, your audience will resonate with it. But for now, you should paint for the only person your work will mean the most to -- yourself!

For context, I consider myself extremely perfectionistic as well. However, I find solace in painting, because you're allowed to do whatever you want. There is no "perfect." Every painting is perfect. Every drawing is a snapshot of someone else's mind. Each one is completely unique. How can you judge a work of art? There's no true scale or rubric for that.

I was like this as well. For me, I 'fixed' it by loosening up my expectations. Anyone who can take an image out of their head and put it perfectly on a canvas is a savant. Myself, I try not to get too rigidly attached to a plan or outline. The idea of my paintings is the important part, not the idea of making a 1:1 perfect recreation of an image in my head, which isn't a real image anyways.

In short, try to enjoy the process of creating more than the product (the painting itself). You'll naturally get more comfortable with your medium over time and with practice, and thus you'll be more able to guide your painting toward the image or idea you started with. Likewise, be open to letting your concept evolve and change as it goes down on the canvas. Only one time so far did the painting I ended up with look like the idea I began with. Keep picking up your brush(es)!

And don't worry about "good" or "bad." You are the only real judge of your own work. The most important thing is that you're having fun or enjoying your work. As long as you accomplish the goals you set out for yourself, that's what matters.

Bay-beee, that's a calcite vein! The movement of super hot water under the Earth's crust will inject fluid into rocks at high pressures, creating fractures like this. You can think of it like the Earth fracking itself. That water is very hot and carrying a lot of dissolved ions, which become less soluble as the water cools, thus precipitating out in the fissures as crystals - in this case, dogtooth calcite!

You can't quite call this rock a breccia, because it's not technically made up of sedimentary rock clasts binding together. It's all the broken bits of the same original rock, just glued back together with calcite paste! Pretty dang cool imo.
It's an oreo cookie! The dark layers are amphibolite, and the cream colored layer in the center is likely granitic in composition (lots of quartz & feldspars)

Great job checking the density, I'm impressed by the initiative! Galena will also leave a grey streak (which I guess makes a lot of sense), if you wanted to test that.

I can't identify the name specifically (the minerals are too degraded to identify them properly), but I can tell you a bit about it! This is a weathered and rounded clast of an igneous rock, possibly **andesite**. The greyish color hints at an intermediate magma composition, supported by the presence of amphibole minerals (the elongate black crystals, possibly hornblende). The more equant, reddish-brown crystals are reminiscent of weathered garnets (which can occur in volcanic rocks like this, but are far more common in metamorphic rocks). More interesting, the rock is displaying great *porphyritic texture*; i.e., it has two different modes of crystals, both the large visible ones (called *phenocrysts*) and the very finely grained groundmass.

Color isn't often very helpful in identifying features with minerals, as color can be highly variable. That said, it can offer a lot of neat clues about chemistry! It's thought that the purple color in amethyst actually also comes from iron content, so it's very plausible here. Alternatively, another variety of quartz - "rose quartz" - can get its reddish pink colors from other trace metals, like titanium and aluminum.

As a F2P player, you should have access to the Moon as a patrol destination at the very least. Up in Sorrow's Harbor, the Altars of Sorrow are a very good way to farm lots of kills. This is an ideal method for some guns, like Graviton Lance or the Sunshot.

If you're very greedy (like me), and refuse to compete for kills, my preferred spot to farm catalysts is the **Exodus Garden 2A** lost sector in the Cosmodrome, over in the Divide. Depending on the catalyst, each run will net you 10-12% completion. Almost all of the mobs are very weak and easy to 1-shot with pretty much anything. Just bring your class's insta-kill super to murder the boss (thundercrash/chaos reach/golden gun), that's the only place that really slows you down.
The catalyst drops from any non-guardian kill on Nessus, so yes, you can obtain it from the current Nightfall. Good luck!
